Available ≠ Accessible / WIC

Getting help buying food shouldn’t be this much work.

WIC
Food benefits
Follow an illustrative parent

WIC—the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children—helps eligible pregnant people, new parents, and children under five get nutritious food.

But getting enrolled is only the beginning.

What else does WIC provide?
Nutrition advice, breastfeeding support, and referrals to care. This parent’s journey is illustrative; the program rules and research are documented.
Start during pregnancy ↓

More than half of eligible pregnant women aren’t receiving WIC.

A prenatal clinic can refer a parent to WIC. The parent still has to enroll.

23.3% · Who didn’t know?
Current adult participants asked why they had not enrolled during earlier pregnancies. Data collected in 2019. Population and methodology ↗
22.6% · Who thought they didn’t qualify?
A separate reason reported by the same surveyed subgroup. Do not add these percentages together. USDA findings ↗
What information do I need?
California asks for proof of identity, residence, and income or participation in a qualifying program. Examples can include identification, mail showing your address, and income records or Medi-Cal information. Ask the agency what is acceptable in your situation; one particular document is not the only route. Requirements and examples ↗
Resources & context
2019 survey; current adult participants explaining nonenrollment during prior pregnancies. Separate reasons, not rejection rates or shares of all eligible families. USDA survey, Exhibit 4 ↗ California enrollment ↗

After birth

The baby arrives. The benefits change.

We now follow a fully breastfeeding postpartum package—one example, not a recommendation. The groceries ahead are for the parent.

WIC
Updated package

Store access · USDA research

A benefit card doesn’t make a store nearby.

1 driving mileUrban access threshold10 driving milesRural access threshold
Schematic illustration · not a household route

40% of estimated WIC-eligible families lacked convenient retailer access.

50 states + DC · FY2022 · USDA proximity analysis
Next scene ↓
How access was measured
USDA measured driving distance from population-weighted census-tract centers: one mile in urban areas and ten miles in rural areas. The eligible-family proxy counts families below 185% of the poverty line with children under five. Forty percent of estimated eligible families lacked convenient access; the separate 45% finding refers to census tracts, not families. This is not a measured journey for the illustrative parent. USDA report, executive summary and Chapter IV. Montebello remains the price source for the shopping example, not the location of this access analysis.

Complete example package and untouched foods

Fully breastfeeding postpartum, no-juice example: 4 gallons milk; 2 dozen eggs; 32 oz cheese; 64 oz yogurt; 36 oz cereal; 48 oz whole grains; 20 oz canned fish; one peanut-butter/bean option plus one additional dry-bean container; and $55 produce ($52 baseline + $3 instead of juice).

This trip used the peanut butter option. Cheese, yogurt, cereal, canned fish and the additional beans remain untouched. Alternatives replace a benefit; they do not add extra food.

10 / Research pause · benefit use

Issued doesn’t always mean used.

First: what counts as high use?
70% threshold

Using at least 70% of the produce benefit during a study certification period.

About 70 in 100 study periods used at least 70% of produce benefits.

Exact result: 69.6% · Southern California · November 2019–June 2023

The marks round the result. This is a share of certification periods—not a percentage of all food dollars spent.
Next scene ↓
Compare food categories

Share of certification periods reaching the same 70% threshold. Categories have different eligible participant groups.

Continued participation: an association
Discontinuation was 61.7% among periods with under 10% overall redemption versus 13.1% among periods with at least 70%. This is observational, not proof that redemption prevents departure. Continued eligibility was not established.
Resources & context
188,368 participants, with repeat certification periods. Category denominators differ: formula 140,789; produce 365,738; eggs 364,908; whole milk 176,981. Study and tables ↗

Resources & context
California certification varies by category and age at enrollment. Infants certified before six months can be certified through the first birthday month; child certification is generally one year. Mid-certification assessments occur in the specified fifth-to-seventh-month window. Pregnancy and postpartum are distinct certifications. Certification periods ↗ Mid-certification policy ↗

Already connected to other help
In a separate survey-based analysis, 41.8% of WIC-eligible children ages 1–4 receiving both Medicaid and SNAP were not receiving WIC. This suggests an opportunity for referrals; it is not additive with the national gap. USDA Table 5.1 ↗
